label: Genesis
short_description: The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world, the origins of humanity, and the earliest history of the people of Israel.
content:
Genesis (Greek: Genesis, Hebrew: Bereshit) is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Its name derives from the Greek word for "origin" or "coming into being," reflecting its central concern with beginnings.

The book opens with two complementary accounts of [[placeholder:"Creation"|"The act by which God brought the world into existence, told across the first two chapters of Genesis"]]. The first account (Genesis 1:1-2:3) presents [[placeholder:"The Seven Days of Creation"|"The structured account of God creating the world in seven days, as told in Genesis 1:1-2:3"]], a liturgical narrative in which [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] brings order from chaos. The second (Genesis 2:4-25) offers a more intimate portrait of human origins in [[placeholder:"The Garden of Eden"|"The primordial garden planted by God in the east, where the first humans lived in innocence before the fall"]].

From creation, Genesis moves through the stories of [[placeholder:"Adam and Eve"|"The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden"]], whose disobedience leads to expulsion from paradise. Their descendants multiply, but so does wickedness, prompting [[placeholder:"The Flood"|"The cataclysmic deluge sent by God to cleanse the earth, survived only by Noah and his family aboard the Ark"]] — a divine reckoning survived only by [[placeholder:"Noah"|"Righteous man chosen by God to survive the great flood and preserve life on earth"]].

The patriarchal narratives follow: [[placeholder:"Abraham"|"Father of the Hebrew nation, called by God to leave his homeland for a promised land"]] is called out of Mesopotamia by God, who makes with him the [[placeholder:"Covenant"|"The binding agreement between God and Abraham promising descendants, land, and blessing"]]. Through Abraham's son [[placeholder:"Isaac"|"Son of Abraham and Sarah, second patriarch of the Israelites"]] and grandson [[placeholder:"Jacob"|"Grandson of Abraham, later named Israel, father of the twelve tribes"]], the promise narrows to a single family. The book closes with [[placeholder:"Joseph"|"Son of Jacob who rose to power in Egypt, enabling the survival of his family during famine"]], whose journey from slavery to the court of Pharaoh brings the family of Israel to Egypt.

Genesis spans from the creation of the cosmos to the death of Joseph in Egypt, covering themes of divine sovereignty, covenant, human failing, and the persistent faithfulness of God toward the people he has chosen.

label: The Seven Days of Creation
short_description: The structured account of God creating the world in seven days, as told in Genesis 1:1-2:3, moving from primordial chaos to ordered cosmos.
content:
The opening chapter of [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]] presents creation as a seven-day sequence in which [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] fashions the world from formless void. The narrative follows a deliberate literary structure: the first three days establish domains, and the next three fill them with inhabitants.

## The Days

**Day 1** — God creates [[placeholder:"Light"|"The first thing God creates, separated from darkness to form day and night"]] and separates it from [[placeholder:"Darkness"|"The primordial state before creation; separated from light on the first day"]]. "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light."

**Day 2** — God creates the [[placeholder:"Firmament"|"The expanse or dome that separates the waters above from the waters below, called Heaven"]], dividing the waters above from the waters below.

**Day 3** — The waters are gathered, and [[placeholder:"Dry Land"|"The earth that appears when God gathers the waters together on the third day"]] appears. Vegetation springs forth: grass, herbs, and fruit trees.

**Day 4** — God sets the [[placeholder:"Sun"|"The greater light set in the firmament to rule the day"]] and [[placeholder:"Moon"|"The lesser light set in the firmament to rule the night"]] in the firmament to govern day and night and to mark seasons.

**Day 5** — The seas fill with living creatures and the skies with birds. God blesses them: "Be fruitful, and multiply."

**Day 6** — God creates land animals, and then humanity: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." [[placeholder:"Adam and Eve"|"The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden"]] are given dominion over all living things.

**Day 7** — God rests, blessing and sanctifying the seventh day. This becomes the basis for the [[placeholder:"Sabbath"|"The seventh day of rest, sanctified by God after the completion of creation"]].

## Structure and Symmetry

The days pair symmetrically: Day 1 (light/dark) corresponds to Day 4 (luminaries); Day 2 (sky/sea) to Day 5 (birds/fish); Day 3 (land/plants) to Day 6 (animals/humans). This chiastic structure suggests a carefully composed literary work rather than a chronological report.

The repeated refrain "And God saw that it was good" punctuates each act of creation, culminating in "very good" after the creation of humanity on Day 6.

label: The Garden of Eden
short_description: The primordial garden planted by God in the east, where the first humans lived in innocence before the fall.
content:
The Garden of Eden appears in [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]] chapters 2-3 as the setting for humanity's origin and first crisis. After forming [[placeholder:"Adam and Eve"|"The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden"]] from the dust of the ground, [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] plants a garden "eastward in Eden" and places the man there to tend it.

## Geography

Genesis describes a river flowing out of Eden to water the garden, dividing into four branches: the [[placeholder:"Pishon"|"One of the four rivers of Eden, said to wind through the land of Havilah"]], the [[placeholder:"Gihon"|"One of the four rivers of Eden, encompassing the land of Cush"]], the [[placeholder:"Tigris"|"The third river of Eden, flowing east of Assyria"]], and the [[placeholder:"Euphrates"|"The fourth river of Eden, the great river of Mesopotamia"]]. The mention of the Tigris and Euphrates anchors the mythic geography in the real landscape of [[placeholder:"Mesopotamia"|"The ancient region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, cradle of early civilization"]].

## The Two Trees

Two trees stand at the center of the garden: the Tree of Life and the [[placeholder:"Tree of Knowledge"|"The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, whose fruit God forbade the first humans to eat"]]. God permits the man to eat from any tree except the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, warning that eating from it will bring death.

The [[placeholder:"Serpent"|"The craftiest of the animals in Eden, who tempts Eve to eat the forbidden fruit"]], described as more cunning than any beast of the field, persuades the woman to eat the forbidden fruit. She eats and gives some to the man. Their eyes are opened; they know they are naked and hide from God.

## The Expulsion

God confronts them, and the consequences follow: the serpent is cursed to crawl on its belly, the woman will bear children in pain, and the man will toil for his food from ground that is now cursed. God makes garments of skin for them and drives them from the garden, stationing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life.

The expulsion from Eden marks the beginning of human history outside paradise — a theme that reverberates through the stories of [[placeholder:"Cain and Abel"|"The first sons of Adam and Eve; Cain murders Abel in the first act of fratricide"]], [[placeholder:"The Flood"|"The cataclysmic deluge sent by God to cleanse the earth, survived only by Noah and his family aboard the Ark"]], and the long arc of the patriarchs.

label: Adam and Eve
short_description: The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden, whose disobedience brought about the fall.
content:
Adam and Eve are the first human beings in [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]]. Their story, told in Genesis 2-3, is the Bible's account of how humanity began and how it fell.

## Creation

In the second creation account, [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] forms Adam (Hebrew: 'adam, "human" or "earth-creature") from the dust of the ground and breathes life into his nostrils. God places him in [[placeholder:"The Garden of Eden"|"The primordial garden planted by God in the east, where the first humans lived in innocence before the fall"]] to tend and keep it.

Finding that "it is not good for the man to be alone," God creates the animals and brings them to Adam to name — the first act of human language and dominion. None proves a suitable companion, so God fashions Eve from Adam's side. "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh," Adam declares.

## The Fall

The [[placeholder:"Serpent"|"The craftiest of the animals in Eden, who tempts Eve to eat the forbidden fruit"]] persuades Eve to eat from the [[placeholder:"Tree of Knowledge"|"The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, whose fruit God forbade the first humans to eat"]], promising that she will become "like God, knowing good and evil." She eats and shares the fruit with Adam. Their innocence is shattered — they see their nakedness and hide from God.

God's judgment falls on all three: the serpent is cursed, Eve will bear children in pain, and Adam will labor against cursed ground until he returns to dust. They are expelled from Eden, cut off from the Tree of Life.

## Legacy

Outside the garden, Eve bears [[placeholder:"Cain and Abel"|"The first sons of Adam and Eve; Cain murders Abel in the first act of fratricide"]], and through their descendants the human race spreads across the earth. The line from Adam through [[placeholder:"Seth"|"Third son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel"]] eventually leads to [[placeholder:"Noah"|"Righteous man chosen by God to survive the great flood and preserve life on earth"]], and from Noah through the patriarchs to [[placeholder:"Abraham"|"Father of the Hebrew nation, called by God to leave his homeland for a promised land"]].

Adam and Eve embody the paradox at the heart of Genesis: humanity is made in the image of God, yet continually chooses its own way. Their story establishes the pattern of sin, consequence, and divine grace that runs through the entire biblical narrative.

label: Noah and the Flood
short_description: The account of the great deluge in Genesis 6-9, in which God destroys a corrupt world but preserves Noah, his family, and the animals aboard the Ark.
content:
The story of Noah and the Flood (Genesis 6-9) is the great crisis of [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]] — a divine undoing of [[placeholder:"Creation"|"The act by which God brought the world into existence, told across the first two chapters of Genesis"]] followed by a new beginning.

## The Corruption

By the time of [[placeholder:"Noah"|"Righteous man chosen by God to survive the great flood and preserve life on earth"]], the descendants of [[placeholder:"Adam and Eve"|"The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden"]] have filled the earth, but "every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually." [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] regrets making humanity and resolves to wipe the slate clean.

Noah alone "found favor in the eyes of the Lord" — a righteous man in a corrupt generation. God instructs him to build an ark of gopher wood, three hundred cubits long, and to bring aboard his family and pairs of every living creature.

## The Deluge

The floodwaters come from two directions: the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the windows of heaven are opened. For forty days and nights the rain falls, and the waters prevail upon the earth for a hundred and fifty days. Every living thing outside the ark perishes. The flood is a reversal of the separation of waters on Day 2 of [[placeholder:"The Seven Days of Creation"|"The structured account of God creating the world in seven days, as told in Genesis 1:1-2:3"]] — the boundaries between sky-water and earth-water collapse.

## The Recession

God remembers Noah. A wind passes over the earth, the waters recede, and the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove; when the dove returns with an olive branch, he knows the waters have abated. The family and animals emerge onto dry ground.

## The Covenant

Noah builds an altar and offers sacrifices. God makes a [[placeholder:"Covenant"|"The binding agreement between God and Abraham promising descendants, land, and blessing"]] with Noah and all living creatures: never again will a flood destroy the earth. The rainbow is set in the sky as the sign of this promise.

God blesses Noah and his sons with the same words given to [[placeholder:"Adam and Eve"|"The first human beings in the Genesis narrative, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden"]]: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth." Creation begins again.

## After the Flood

Noah plants a vineyard — the first act of agriculture in the new world — and becomes drunk. The incident with his son Ham introduces the curse of Canaan, foreshadowing the conflicts that will define later Israelite history. From Noah's three sons — Shem, Ham, and Japheth — the nations of the earth descend, leading eventually to [[placeholder:"Abraham"|"Father of the Hebrew nation, called by God to leave his homeland for a promised land"]] in the line of Shem.

label: Abraham
short_description: Father of the Hebrew nation, called by God out of Mesopotamia to receive the promise of descendants, land, and blessing.
content:
Abraham (originally Abram) is the central figure of the patriarchal narratives in [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]]. His story (Genesis 12-25) marks a turning point: after the universal narratives of [[placeholder:"Creation"|"The act by which God brought the world into existence, told across the first two chapters of Genesis"]], the Fall, and [[placeholder:"The Flood"|"The cataclysmic deluge sent by God to cleanse the earth, survived only by Noah and his family aboard the Ark"]], God narrows his focus to one man and one family.

## The Call

"Go from your country, your kindred, and your father's house to the land that I will show you." [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] calls Abram out of [[placeholder:"Mesopotamia"|"The ancient region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, cradle of early civilization"]] — specifically from Ur of the Chaldeans, through Haran — toward an unknown destination. The promise is threefold: a great nation, a blessed name, and blessing to all the families of the earth.

Abram goes, at the age of seventy-five, with his wife Sarai and his nephew [[placeholder:"Lot"|"Nephew of Abraham who settled near Sodom; his story intertwines with Abraham's throughout Genesis"]].

## The Covenant

God makes a [[placeholder:"Covenant"|"The binding agreement between God and Abraham promising descendants, land, and blessing"]] with Abraham in stages. In Genesis 15, the covenant is sealed with a mysterious ceremony: animals are cut in half, and a smoking fire pot passes between the pieces. In Genesis 17, God renames Abram to Abraham ("father of many nations") and Sarai to Sarah, and institutes circumcision as the covenant sign.

The central tension: Abraham is promised descendants as numerous as the stars, but Sarah is barren and both are old.

## Isaac

Against all natural possibility, Sarah bears [[placeholder:"Isaac"|"Son of Abraham and Sarah, second patriarch of the Israelites"]] in their old age. The promised son becomes the vehicle for the covenant's continuation.

Then comes the most harrowing test: God commands Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22). Abraham obeys, binding Isaac on the altar, but at the last moment an angel stays his hand and a ram is provided instead. "Now I know that you fear God," the angel says.

## Legacy

Abraham dies at 175, "an old man, full of years." Through Isaac and [[placeholder:"Jacob"|"Grandson of Abraham, later named Israel, father of the twelve tribes"]], the covenant promise continues to narrow toward the people who will become Israel. Abraham's faith — his willingness to leave everything known for an unseen promise — becomes the defining model of trust in God throughout the biblical tradition.

label: Joseph in Egypt
short_description: The story of Jacob's favored son, sold into slavery by his brothers, who rises to become vizier of Egypt and saves his family from famine.
content:
The Joseph narrative (Genesis 37-50) closes the book of [[placeholder:"Genesis"|"The first book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the creation of the world and the earliest history of Israel"]] with its longest and most literary story — a tale of betrayal, providence, and reconciliation that brings the family of Israel from Canaan to Egypt.

## The Favored Son

[[placeholder:"Joseph"|"Son of Jacob who rose to power in Egypt, enabling the survival of his family during famine"]] is the eleventh son of [[placeholder:"Jacob"|"Grandson of Abraham, later named Israel, father of the twelve tribes"]] and the first son of Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife. Jacob shows him open favoritism, giving him the famous "coat of many colors" (or "long-sleeved robe"). Joseph's dreams — in which his brothers' sheaves bow to his, and the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him — inflame their jealousy.

## Slavery and Rise

The brothers sell Joseph to a caravan of merchants heading to Egypt. They dip his coat in goat's blood and tell Jacob his son is dead. In Egypt, Joseph serves in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, where he prospers until Potiphar's wife falsely accuses him. He is thrown into prison.

In prison, Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. Two years later, when Pharaoh himself has troubling dreams — seven fat cows devoured by seven lean cows, seven plump ears of grain consumed by seven thin ones — the cupbearer remembers Joseph. Joseph interprets the dreams as seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine, and advises Pharaoh to store grain.

Pharaoh appoints Joseph vizier of Egypt, second only to Pharaoh himself. Joseph is thirty years old.

## The Reunion

When the famine strikes, it reaches Canaan. Jacob sends his sons to Egypt to buy grain — unknowingly sending them to their brother. Joseph recognizes them but conceals his identity, testing them through a series of increasingly charged encounters.

The turning point comes when [[placeholder:"Judah"|"Fourth son of Jacob, who offers himself as a substitute for Benjamin and becomes ancestor of the royal line"]] offers himself as a slave in place of the youngest brother Benjamin. Joseph, overcome, reveals himself: "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" The brothers are terrified, but Joseph reassures them: "You intended to harm me, but [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] intended it for good, to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives."

## The Family in Egypt

Jacob and the entire family — seventy persons — come down to Egypt and settle in the land of Goshen. Before his death, Jacob blesses each of his twelve sons, establishing the identities of the [[placeholder:"Twelve Tribes of Israel"|"The twelve tribal groups descended from Jacob's sons, forming the people of Israel"]]. Joseph makes his brothers swear to carry his bones back to Canaan when [[placeholder:"God"|"The deity of the Hebrew Bible, referred to as Elohim and YHWH"]] eventually brings them home.

Genesis ends with Joseph's death in Egypt at 110 years old, embalmed and placed in a coffin — the family of [[placeholder:"Abraham"|"Father of the Hebrew nation, called by God to leave his homeland for a promised land"]] now far from the promised land, awaiting a future deliverance.
